sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Transportation questions cover the shape of a road, how traffic moves along it, the signs and signals that control it, the pavement underneath and how demand is forecast.

Geometric design questions come down to what a driver can see and how quickly a vehicle can stop or turn at the design speed.
pitfalls: Using mph in a formula that expects ft/s, or the reverse. The 1.47 factor converts mph to ft/s.
Entering grades as percentages where the formula expects decimals.

Pavement thickness depends on truck loads and the soil beneath.

sections.title: Geometric design
sections.body:
Geometric design sets the shape of a road so drivers can see far enough and vehicles stay on it at the design speed. Stopping sight distance is the distance covered during perception and reaction plus the braking distance.

Horizontal curves are arcs of circles. Their minimum radius depends on speed, superelevation (banking) and side friction. Vertical curves are parabolas joining two grades. Crest curves are sized so the hilltop does not hide the road ahead, and sag curves for headlight reach. The rate of vertical curvature K is the curve length per percent change in grade.

formulas.name: Curve length
formulas.expr: L = R × deflection angle in radians

formulas.name: Vertical curve
formulas.expr: L = KA, high or low point at x = g_{1}L / (g_{1} - g_{2})

pitfalls: Entering superelevation as a percent instead of a decimal.
Using a downgrade as positive: a downgrade lengthens the stopping distance.
Putting mph into a formula that expects ft/s, or the reverse. Stopping sight distance takes mph; the yellow interval takes ft/s.
Entering grades as percentages where the formula expects decimals.

ideas.title: Chord, not arc
ideas.text: A straight sight line from the PC to the PT is the long chord, 2 R sin(I / 2), not the curve length, even when the question never says chord.

ideas.title: Degree of curve
ideas.text: By the arc definition, the degree of curve is the central angle subtended by 100 ft of arc, so R = 5,729.58 / D.

ideas.title: Stations are 100 ft units
ideas.text: A station of 8+00 is 800 ft along the alignment. Convert to feet, do the arithmetic (PC = PI - T, PT = PC + L), then write the result back as a station.

ideas.title: Two straight lines to the end of a vertical curve
ideas.text: The PVI sits at half the curve length. The PVT elevation is the PVC elevation plus the first grade over L / 2 plus the second grade over L / 2. Elevations on the curve itself need the parabola, and the high or low point is usually not at mid-curve.

ideas.title: What sets the length of a crest curve
ideas.text: A driver's eye 3.5 ft above the road must see a 2 ft object over the crest at the stopping sight distance. Compute that distance for the downgrade, where gravity works against braking, then find the length from the sight distance and the grade change.

ideas.title: Where 1.47 comes from
ideas.text: 5,280 ft per mile over 3,600 s per hour is 1.47, which is why a speed in mph times a time in seconds, times 1.47, gives feet.

ideas.title: Stopping sight distance
ideas.text: Stopping sight distance has two parts: the distance covered at full speed during perception and reaction, 1.47 V t, and the braking distance, V^{2} / (30 (a/32.2 ± G)). With V in mph the constants give feet. On a level road the grade term G is zero.

ideas.title: Horizontal curves
ideas.text: On a horizontal curve the centripetal force is supplied by superelevation and side friction together. Balancing them gives the minimum radius R = V^{2} / (15 (e + f)), with V in mph, R in feet and e as a decimal.

ideas.title: Vertical curves
ideas.text: A vertical curve is a parabola, so its grade changes at a constant rate r = (g_{2} - g_{1}) / L. The high or low point is where the grade reaches zero: x = -g_{1} / r = g_{1} L / (g_{1} - g_{2}).

ideas.title: Horizontal curves
ideas.text: The length of a circular curve is the arc subtended by the deflection (central) angle: L = R × angle in radians = R × Δ × π / 180.

ideas.title: Horizontal curves
ideas.text: The two tangents meet at the PI. Each tangent, from PC to PI or PI to PT, has length T = R tan(Δ / 2), from the right triangle formed by the radius, the tangent and the line from the centre to the PI.

ideas.title: Vertical curves
ideas.text: K is the horizontal length of curve needed for each 1% of grade change, chosen from the design speed to provide sight distance. Curve length = K × A, where A is the algebraic difference in grades in percent.

ideas.title: Horizontal curves
ideas.text: The PC lies one tangent length back from the PI, and T = R tan(I / 2). Stations are 100 ft units, so work in feet and convert at the end.

ideas.title: Vertical curves
ideas.text: The PVI sits at half the curve length. From the PVC, follow the first grade for L / 2 to the PVI, then the second grade for L / 2 to the PVT. The curve itself is not needed for the end points.

ideas.title: Vertical curves
ideas.text: On a crest, the hill itself blocks the driver's view. For a 3.5 ft eye height and a 2 ft object, with the sight distance shorter than the curve, L = A S^{2} / 2,158, where A is the algebraic difference in grades in percent. Check afterwards that S is less than L.

ideas.title: Horizontal curves
ideas.text: By the arc definition, the degree of curve is the central angle subtended by 100 ft of arc. A full circle of 360° has a circumference of 2πR, which gives R = 5,729.58 / D.

examples.steps:
A = 2.5 + 2.0 = 4.5%.

L = \frac{4.5(700)^{2}}{2,158} = 1,022 ft. This is longer than 700 ft, so the assumption holds.

sections.deep:
Geometric design fits the road to what drivers and vehicles can do at the design speed. Sight distance comes first: a driver must be able to see far enough to stop. Stopping sight distance is the distance travelled during perception and reaction plus the braking distance.

Horizontal curves balance centripetal force with superelevation and side friction, which sets the minimum radius. Curve geometry follows from the radius and deflection angle: tangent length, curve length, external and middle ordinate. Vertical curves are parabolas joining two grades; their length is set by sight distance through the K value, and the high or low point is where the grade is zero.
method: Identify the element: sight distance, horizontal curve or vertical curve.
For sight distance, add the reaction and braking terms, with grade in the braking term.
For a horizontal curve, compute T, L and stationing of PC and PT from the PI.
For a vertical curve, compute A, the rate of grade change, elevations along the curve and the turning point.
Keep U.S. units straight: speeds in mph, lengths in ft, grades in percent or decimal as the formula requires.

side friction

deflection angle

sections.title: Pavement system design
sections.body:
A pavement spreads wheel loads so the soil underneath is not overstressed. Flexible (asphalt) pavements do it with layers that get stronger toward the top. Rigid (concrete) pavements do it with a stiff slab.

Traffic is counted in equivalent single axle loads (ESALs): every axle is converted to the number of standard 18,000 lb axles that would do the same damage. Heavy axles do far more damage than light ones. In the AASHTO method the structural number sums each layer's thickness times its strength coefficient. The subgrade is described by its resilient modulus or CBR. Drainage and timely rehabilitation extend pavement life.

formulas.name: Design ESALs
formulas.expr: daily ESALs × 365 × years (with a growth factor if traffic grows)

pitfalls: Leaving out the drainage coefficients for unbound layers.

example.problem: A pavement has 5 in of asphalt (a = 0.44) over 10 in of base (a = 0.14, m = 1.0). Find the structural number.

ideas.title: ESALs from an axle table
ideas.text: Each axle load has a load equivalency factor that expresses its damage relative to an 18-kip single axle. Multiply each axle's factor by its number of passes and add; single and tandem axles have separate tables.

ideas.title: Subgrade and subbase
ideas.text: The subgrade is the soil already there, prepared and compacted. The subbase is a placed layer between it and the base. A structural number equation can also be solved backwards for the thickness of one layer.

ideas.title: Structural number
ideas.text: In the AASHTO flexible pavement method, each layer contributes its thickness times a layer coefficient that reflects its relative strength, and unbound layers are also multiplied by a drainage coefficient. The sum is the structural number, SN.

The resilient modulus describes subgrade stiffness under repeated wheel loads and is the subgrade input to pavement design. For fine-grained soils with low CBR it is often estimated from the correlation M_{R} = 1,500 × CBR, in psi.

ideas.title: ESAL
ideas.text: Pavement design uses the total number of 18-kip equivalent single axle loads over the design life. With no growth it is the daily ESALs × 365 × years.

examples.problem: A flexible pavement has 5 in of asphalt (layer coefficient 0.44), 10 in of base (0.14) and 8 in of subbase (0.11). Drainage coefficients are 1.0. What is the structural number?
examples.idea: In the AASHTO flexible pavement method, each layer contributes its thickness times a layer coefficient that reflects its relative strength, and unbound layers are also multiplied by a drainage coefficient. The sum is the structural number, SN.

examples.problem: Using the correlation M_{R} = 1,500 × CBR (psi), what is the resilient modulus of a subgrade with a CBR of 7?
examples.idea: The resilient modulus describes subgrade stiffness under repeated wheel loads and is the subgrade input to pavement design. For fine-grained soils with low CBR it is often estimated from the correlation M_{R} = 1,500 × CBR, in psi.

examples.problem: A highway lane carries 950 equivalent single axle loads (ESALs) per day with no growth. How many ESALs does it carry over a 20-year design life?
examples.idea: Pavement design uses the total number of 18-kip equivalent single axle loads over the design life. With no growth it is the daily ESALs × 365 × years.

examples.problem: A flexible pavement needs a structural number of 4.3. It will have 5.2 in of asphalt with a layer coefficient of 0.44, on a granular base with a layer coefficient of 0.14 and a drainage coefficient of 1.0. How thick must the base be?
examples.idea: The AASHTO structural number is the sum, over the layers, of layer coefficient × thickness × drainage coefficient. Subtract what the asphalt provides and divide the remainder by the base's coefficient times its drainage coefficient.

examples.problem: A road carries 12,750 vehicles per day, of which 14% are trucks with an average truck factor of 0.9 ESALs per truck. Half the traffic uses the design lane. How many ESALs does the design lane receive in one year?
examples.idea: Pavement damage is counted in equivalent 18-kip single axle loads. Yearly ESALs = daily traffic × truck share × truck factor × 365 × the share in the design lane. Cars are ignored because their damage is negligible.

examples.problem: Using the fourth-power rule, how many passes of an 18-kip single axle do the same pavement damage as one pass of a 21 kip single axle?
examples.idea: Pavement damage rises very steeply with axle load, roughly with the fourth power of the load ratio. A modest overload therefore does several times the damage, which is why weight limits matter.

sections.deep:
A pavement spreads wheel loads so that the subgrade is not overstressed. Flexible pavements do it with layers of decreasing quality; rigid pavements with the bending stiffness of a concrete slab. Traffic is expressed as the number of 18-kip equivalent single axle loads over the design life, because damage rises steeply with axle weight.

The AASHTO method for flexible pavements finds the structural number required for the traffic, subgrade resilient modulus and reliability, then provides it with layer thicknesses times layer and drainage coefficients.
method: Convert traffic to design ESALs.
Find the required structural number from the design chart or equation.
Choose layer thicknesses so that the sum of a × D × m meets it.
Check each layer against the structural number required above the layer beneath.
Round thicknesses up to practical values.

sections.title: Traffic capacity and flow theory
sections.body:
Traffic is described by three linked quantities. Flow is vehicles per hour past a point. Density is vehicles per mile of road. Speed is how fast they move. Flow equals density times speed.

As a road fills, speed drops. Flow peaks at capacity, part-way between empty and jammed. In the Greenshields model that peak is at half the free-flow speed and half the jam density. At signals, capacity is the saturation flow times the share of the cycle that is green. The peak hour factor measures how uneven traffic is within the busiest hour.
pitfalls: Confusing time mean speed with space mean speed. The flow relation uses space mean speed.
Using all lanes of a 'six-lane' freeway. N is the number of lanes in one direction, three in that case.

ideas.title: Finding the peak hour in 15-minute counts
ideas.text: Add each run of four consecutive 15-minute counts. The largest total is the peak hour volume, and the peak hour factor uses the largest 15-minute count inside that hour.

ideas.title: Freeway level of service
ideas.text: Convert the hourly volume to a flow rate per lane: v_{p} = V / (PHF × N × f_{HV}), with the heavy vehicle factor f_{HV} = 1 / (1 + P_{T}(E_{T} - 1)). Density is v_{p} divided by speed, and the level of service table is entered with density.

ideas.title: Traffic flow relationships
ideas.text: The fundamental relation of traffic flow: flow = density × space mean speed (q = k u). The units confirm it: veh/mi × mi/h = veh/h.

ideas.title: Peak hour factor
ideas.text: The peak hour factor compares the hourly volume with the flow rate of the busiest 15 minutes: PHF = V / (4 × V_{15}). A value of 1.0 means perfectly even flow; lower values mean sharper peaking. Dividing a volume by the PHF gives the design flow rate.

ideas.title: Saturation flow
ideas.text: A signalized lane group can only discharge during its effective green. Capacity is the saturation flow rate times the share of the cycle that is green: c = N s (g / C).

ideas.title: Traffic flow relationships
ideas.text: Greenshields assumes speed falls linearly with density. Flow = density × speed is then a parabola that peaks at half the jam density and half the free-flow speed, so capacity = u_{f} k_{j} / 4.

ideas.title: Traffic flow relationships
ideas.text: Convert the volume to an equivalent passenger car flow rate per lane: divide by the peak hour factor, the number of lanes in that direction and the heavy vehicle factor, f_{HV} = 1 / (1 + P_{T}(E_{T} - 1)). Density is flow rate over speed.

examples.problem: Three vehicles cross a short road section at 35, 42 and 58 mph. What is the space mean speed?
examples.idea: Space mean speed is the harmonic mean of the individual speeds: the number of vehicles divided by the sum of 1 / speed. It is the speed that ties flow to density, and it is never more than the arithmetic (time) mean.
examples.steps: Space mean speed = \frac{3}{\frac{1}{35} + \frac{1}{42} + \frac{1}{58}} = \frac{3}{0.06962} = 43.09 mph. The arithmetic mean is 45.00 mph.

sections.deep:
Traffic flow is described by three linked quantities: flow (vehicles per hour), speed and density (vehicles per mile), with flow = speed × density. As density rises, speed falls. Under the Greenshields model the fall is linear, so flow peaks at half the jam density and half the free-flow speed; that peak is capacity.

Capacity analysis compares demand with capacity as a volume-to-capacity ratio and reports level of service from A to F. The peak hour factor converts an hourly volume to the flow rate of its busiest 15 minutes. At signals, a lane group's capacity is its saturation flow times the share of the cycle that is effectively green.
method: Write down which of flow, speed and density are known.
Use flow = speed × density, and the speed-density relation if given.
For capacity under Greenshields, use free-flow speed × jam density / 4.
Convert volume to flow rate with the peak hour factor.
For a signal, compute capacity as saturation flow × g / C and the v/c ratio.

sections.title: Traffic control devices
sections.body:
Traffic control devices are the signs, signals and markings that regulate, warn and guide road users. The MUTCD sets national standards so they look and mean the same everywhere. Shape and colour carry meaning: red octagon for stop, yellow diamond for warning, white rectangle for regulation, green for guidance, orange for work zones.

Signals assign right of way by time. The yellow change interval lets a driver who cannot stop safely clear the stop line, and an all-red interval clears the intersection. Signals are justified by warrants based on volumes, crashes and pedestrians.
pitfalls: Entering speed in mph where the formula needs ft/s.

example.problem: Find the yellow interval for an approach speed of 59 ft/s (40 mph) on level ground, with t = 1.0 s and a = 10 ft/s^{2}.
example.steps: y = 1.0 + \frac{59}{20} = 3.95 s, rounded up to 4.0 s in practice.

ideas.title: Yellow and all-red
ideas.text: The yellow interval covers the driver's reaction time plus the time to decelerate. The all-red interval that follows lets a vehicle that entered legally on yellow clear the intersection. Reaction time is taken as 1.0 s at signals, against 2.5 s for stopping sight distance.

ideas.title: Sign classes
ideas.text: The MUTCD sorts signs by function, with matching shapes and colours. Regulatory signs give laws and are mostly white rectangles, with the red octagonal STOP and triangular YIELD as exceptions. Warning signs are yellow diamonds. Guide signs are green. Temporary traffic control signs are orange.

ideas.title: Pavement markings
ideas.text: Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions and mark the left edge of divided roads. White lines separate traffic moving the same way and mark the right edge. A broken line may be crossed, a solid line discourages crossing and a double solid line prohibits it.

ideas.title: Signals
ideas.text: A signal is installed only when an engineering study shows that at least one warrant is met, such as vehicle volume, pedestrian volume or crash experience. Meeting a warrant allows a signal; it does not require one.

ideas.title: What every device must do
ideas.text: Fulfil a need, command attention, convey a clear and simple meaning, command respect from road users and give adequate time for a proper response.

ideas.title: Vehicle signal change interval
ideas.text: The yellow interval must cover the driver's reaction time plus the time to decelerate to a stop, so that a driver too close to stop can enter legally: y = t + v / (2a + 2 g G), with v in ft/s. On level ground the grade term is zero.

examples.problem: A signal approach has a speed of 52.5 mph (77 ft/s) on level ground. Using a perception-reaction time of 1.0 s and a deceleration rate of 10 ft/s^{2}, what yellow change interval is needed?
examples.idea: The yellow interval must cover the driver's reaction time plus the time to decelerate to a stop, so that a driver too close to stop can enter legally: y = t + v / (2a + 2 g G), with v in ft/s. On level ground the grade term is zero.

examples.problem: An intersection is 66 ft wide between stop line and far-side conflict point, and the design vehicle is 20 ft long. Approach speed is 44.0 ft/s. Using r = (W + L) / v, what all-red clearance interval is needed?
examples.idea: The all-red interval gives a vehicle that entered at the end of yellow time to clear the intersection. It must cover the crossing width plus the vehicle's own length at the approach speed.

examples.problem: A signal has a total lost time of 13 s per cycle, and the sum of the critical flow ratios is 0.64. Using Webster's formula C = (1.5L + 5) / (1 - Y), what is the optimum cycle length?
examples.idea: Webster's formula balances two effects: short cycles waste a large share of time on lost time at each phase change, and long cycles make stopped vehicles wait. As the critical flow ratios approach 1 the best cycle grows without limit.

examples.problem: A crosswalk is 77 ft long. Using a walking speed of 3.5 ft/s, what pedestrian clearance time is needed?
examples.idea: The pedestrian clearance time lets someone who steps off the kerb at the end of the walk interval finish crossing. It is the crossing distance divided by the walking speed; the MUTCD uses 3.5 ft/s.

sections.deep:
Traffic control devices tell road users what to do, what to watch for and where to go. The MUTCD standardises them so that the same message always looks the same. Signs, markings and signals each have rules for colour, shape and placement.

Signal timing balances competing movements. The yellow change interval covers reaction time plus deceleration, an all-red interval clears the intersection, and pedestrian intervals are set from crossing distance and walking speed. A signal is justified by warrants examined in an engineering study.
method: Classify the device: regulatory, warning or guide.
Recall its standard colour and shape.
For the yellow interval, use reaction time plus speed over twice the deceleration, adjusted for grade.
For pedestrian clearance, divide crossing distance by walking speed.
For installation questions, look for the engineering study and warrants.

sections.title: Transportation planning
sections.body:
Planning forecasts how much travel there will be and where. The classic four-step model asks four questions in order. Trip generation: how many trips start and end in each zone? Trip distribution: where do they go? Mode choice: by car, bus, bike or foot? Trip assignment: by which route?

Trip generation uses rates per home or per unit of floor area. Distribution often uses a gravity model, in which nearer and larger destinations attract more trips. Mode choice often uses a logit model based on the utility of each mode. Safety analysis compares crash rates per million vehicles or vehicle-miles.
pitfalls: Forgetting that rates are per 1,000 ft^{2}, not per ft^{2}.

example.problem: An office of 120,000 ft^{2} generates 11 trips per 1,000 ft^{2} per day. Find its daily trips.

ideas.title: The gravity model as weighted shares
ideas.text: Trips produced in a zone are split among the destination zones in proportion to each destination's attractions times its friction factor, and a socioeconomic factor where one is given. The shares add up to 1, so nearer and larger zones draw more.

ideas.title: Traffic growth
ideas.text: Volumes grow like compound interest: future volume = present volume × (1 + rate)^{years}.

ideas.title: Trip generation
ideas.text: Trip generation, the first step of the four-step planning model, estimates trip ends from land use. With an average rate, trips = rate × number of units.

ideas.title: Crash rate
ideas.text: Crash rates normalise crash counts by exposure so that sites with different volumes can be compared. For intersections: rate = crashes × 1,000,000 / (ADT × 365 × years).

ideas.title: Logit
ideas.text: The multinomial logit model gives each mode a share proportional to e raised to its utility: P(mode) = e^{U} / (sum of e^{U} over all modes). Only differences in utility matter.

ideas.title: Single payment compound amount
ideas.text: Traffic growth compounds like interest: future volume = present volume × (1 + rate)^{years}. The factor is the single payment compound amount factor from engineering economics.

ideas.title: Gravity model
ideas.text: The gravity model splits a zone's trip productions among destinations in proportion to each destination's attractions times its friction factor. The shares sum to 1.

examples.problem: A subdivision has 320 dwelling units. The trip generation rate is 8.5 trips per dwelling unit per day. How many daily trips does it generate?
examples.idea: Trip generation, the first step of the four-step planning model, estimates trip ends from land use. With an average rate, trips = rate × number of units.

examples.problem: An intersection has 15 crashes in one year. Its entering volume is 27,500 vehicles per day. What is the crash rate per million entering vehicles?
examples.idea: Crash rates normalise crash counts by exposure so that sites with different volumes can be compared. For intersections: rate = crashes × 1,000,000 / (ADT × 365 × years).
examples.steps:
Entering vehicles in one year = 27,500 × 365 = 10,037,500.

Rate = \frac{15 × 1,000,000}{10,037,500} = 1.49 crashes per million entering vehicles.

examples.problem: A logit mode choice model gives a utility of -0.4 for auto and -1.3 for bus. What share of travellers choose the bus?
examples.idea: The multinomial logit model gives each mode a share proportional to e raised to its utility: P(mode) = e^{U} / (sum of e^{U} over all modes). Only differences in utility matter.

examples.problem: A road carries 15,500 vehicles per day. Traffic grows at 2.5% per year. What daily volume is expected in 20 years?
examples.idea: Traffic growth compounds like interest: future volume = present volume × (1 + rate)^{years}. The factor is the single payment compound amount factor from engineering economics.

examples.problem: A zone produces 1,800 trips. Three destination zones have attractions of 350, 450 and 200 and friction factors of 6, 3 and 8. Using the gravity model with K = 1, how many trips go to the first destination?
examples.idea: The gravity model splits a zone's trip productions among destinations in proportion to each destination's attractions times its friction factor. The shares sum to 1.
examples.steps:
A × F for each zone: 2,100, 1,350 and 1,600; sum = 5,050.

Trips to the first = 1,800 × \frac{2,100}{5,050} = 749.

examples.problem: A site had 24 crashes in the study period. A countermeasure with a crash reduction factor of 28% is planned. The ADT was 12,750 before and is forecast at 14,550 after. How many crashes are expected to be prevented?
examples.idea: Crashes prevented = expected crashes without the improvement × crash reduction factor × (ADT after / ADT before). The traffic ratio scales the benefit to the exposure in the period being forecast.

sections.deep:
Transportation planning forecasts travel so that facilities can be sized. The four-step model asks, in order: how many trips are made (trip generation), where they go (trip distribution, often with a gravity model), by which mode (mode choice, often a logit model) and by which route (traffic assignment).

Safety analysis is the other planning tool on the exam: crash rates normalise counts by exposure, per million entering vehicles at intersections and per hundred million vehicle-miles on segments, and crash reduction factors estimate the benefit of a countermeasure.
method: Identify which of the four steps the question concerns.
For generation, multiply the rate by the number of units.
For the gravity model, share trips in proportion to attractions and friction factors.
For logit, compute e to the utility for each mode and divide by the sum.
For crash rates, divide crashes by exposure and scale to the stated basis.
